strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap from Zaremba et al. (2025): why inference-time compute defenses fail against gradient-based/multimodal attacks, and proposes a plausible unifying explanation (the RICH hypothesis) tied to compositional generalization.

Reasonably broad set of complementary experiments: explicit vs. implicit security specifications, white-box PGD attacks at varying epsilon, naive prompt-based compute scaling, CoT-based scaling on Attack-Bard, and extension to large open-source VLMs (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B) to rule out scale as a confound.

Provides some statistically-tested results (McNemar's test) for the CoT/Attack-Bard experiments (Tables 3-4), and qualitative/interpretability evidence (attention maps, attack image changes in Figure 1) that is intuitive and illustrative.

Offers actionable, practical guidance (layering lightweight adversarial finetuning with test-time compute) that could be useful for practitioners, and reframes prior negative findings in a constructive way.
Clear writing structure with explicit hypotheses, predictions, and dedicated 'takeaway' boxes after each experiment aiding readability.
weaknesses: Central claims rest on very small sample sizes in key ablations (e.g., Table 1 uses only 2 replicates; Section 4.2/4.3 use only 4 base images across 3 attack variants = 12 conditions), which is weak evidence for the strong causal 'rich-get-richer' narrative being advanced.

The core finding risks being somewhat tautological: models adversarially trained on gradient-based perturbations are, by construction, more robust to similar gradient attacks and better preserve instruction-following, so it is unsurprising that prompting/compute scaling has more headroom to exploit on top of already-robust base representations. The paper does not clearly disentangle 'compositional generalization enabling specification-following' from the simpler explanation that adversarial training directly improves robust perception/representations, independent of any specification-following mechanism.

The RICH hypothesis is qualitative and not made operationally precise (e.g., no explicit distance metric quantifying 'closeness' of attacked data components to training distribution), limiting its falsifiability and predictive precision beyond directionally-consistent trends.

Evidence for the compositional-generalization mechanism itself is largely anecdotal (a single qualitative example in Figure 1's attention maps) rather than a systematic mechanistic analysis (e.g., probing, representation similarity, or ablations isolating instruction-following from perceptual robustness).

Model diversity is narrow: nearly all core experiments use the same LLaVA-v1.5 architecture family with varying degrees of adversarial training, rather than a broader set of independent architectures/robustification methods, limiting generalizability claims.

The large-scale VLM results (Table 4) show no significant CoT benefit even on clean data in one case and no benefit on adversarial data for both large models, which somewhat undercuts the paper's practical relevance since most large-scale/frontier models are not adversarially pretrained and the approach seems to require costly adversarial training to unlock any benefit.

No comparison to alternative or competing defense/compute-scaling baselines (e.g., other prompting strategies, ensembling, or certified defenses), making it hard to judge the practical significance of the proposed synthesis relative to existing alternatives.

Compute-scaling operationalizations (naive prompt repetition K times, CoT with fixed token budgets) are somewhat ad hoc proxies for 'inference compute' and diverge from the RL-tuned extended reasoning studied in the motivating prior work, raising questions about how well conclusions transfer to true RL-based reasoning scaling in frontier models.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important gap: why inference-time compute defenses (à la Zaremba et al. 2025) fail against gradient-based/multimodal attacks, and what conditions restore their benefit.

Broad experimental scope: multiple model families with varying levels of adversarial training (LLaVA-v1.5, FARE-LLaVA, Delta2LLaVA, InternVL 3.5, Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B), multiple attack types (black-box transfer, white-box PGD at varying epsilon), and multiple inference-scaling strategies (naive specification repetition, CoT, budget-forced reasoning).

Thoughtful control experiments that attempt to rule out confounds, e.g., testing random-token prefill/padding vs. specification-consistent content, and varying the attack budget to test the 'distance to training distribution' mechanism.

Provides some qualitative/interpretability evidence (attention maps, reasoning trace content, attack image visualizations) that adds plausibility to the proposed compositional-generalization mechanism beyond pure aggregate metrics.

Practical, actionable takeaway: even lightweight adversarial finetuning of a vision encoder can be enough to unlock the benefits of test-time compute scaling, which is a useful and reasonably well-supported practical recommendation.
weaknesses: The central hypothesis (RICH) is somewhat unsurprising/incremental: that inference-time defenses work better when the base model is already more robust/generalizes better is close to a restatement of known synergy between train-time and test-time robustness, rather than a sharply novel mechanistic claim.

Statistical power is weak in several key experiments: e.g., Table 2 uses only 2 replicates, Tables 3/7/8 use only 3-4 images, undermining confidence in the reported trends, especially given the qualitative/rhetorical framing ('rich-get-richer') applied to fairly small numeric differences (e.g., Figure 1's ~29%→31.5% accuracy shift).

The models compared (LLaVA-v1.5, FARE, Delta2) differ not only in robustness level but in vision encoder, pretraining data, and instruction-tuning pipeline; the paper does not fully rule out that these confounds (rather than 'robustness' per se) drive the observed differences in inference-time-compute benefit.

The mechanistic claim (compositional generalization) is inferred largely qualitatively (attention maps, reasoning trace counts) rather than directly and rigorously measured/quantified, leaving the causal story more asserted than demonstrated.

Results for large-scale models (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Llama-3.2-Vision-90B) are mixed/weak and somewhat undercut the 'model scale doesn't explain it' argument (e.g., Llama shows no CoT benefit even on clean data), yet this is not discussed as a limitation in depth.

The paper only studies vision-language models and visual attacks; it does not revisit the original text-jailbreak setting from Zaremba et al. to test whether RICH's predictions hold there too, limiting generality of the claimed hypothesis.

Multiple significance tests (McNemar's) are run across many model/condition combinations without correction for multiple comparisons, and some 'benefit' vs 'no benefit' conclusions rest on borderline p-values.

Dense, rhetorically flourished framing (RICH acronym, 'get rich or die scaling') and heavy reliance on informal narrative ('the rich get richer') somewhat obscures precise quantitative claims and effect sizes.
